title: Saffron Walden & Audley End
subtitle: A spice town and a palace
intro: Saturday in north-west Essex. In the morning, Audley End: a huge house built by the man in charge of the king's money. He ended up in the Tower of London. In the afternoon, Saffron Walden: a market town named after a spice.

dayGlance.title: Audley End
dayGlance.sub: 10:00 AM. The house, the horses, the Victorian kitchen and the secret commando school.

dayGlance.title: Saffron Walden
dayGlance.sub: 2:00 PM. The market, Cromwell's headquarters, St Mary's Church and the turf maze.

acts.label: Act 1 · Audley End
acts.narrative: Start at Audley End when it opens. Thomas Howard, the man in charge of King James the First's money, built it to impress the king. Then money went missing, and he ended up in the Tower of London. At 11:15, the horses do a riding display by their 400-year-old stables. In the kitchen is the story of Avis Crocombe, a real Victorian cook who is now famous on YouTube. And in the Second World War, the house was a secret school for Polish paratroopers.

acts.label: Act 2 · Saffron Walden
acts.tagline: The town that saffron made rich.
acts.narrative: Drive 6 minutes to Saffron Walden. It's named after saffron, a spice from a crocus flower. It made the town rich, and the town even changed its name because of it. Then Cromwell's headquarters, the church that saffron money paid for, and a very old maze cut into the grass.

planArrival.title: Home at about 4:50 PM

audley-front.name: Audley End — the front of the house
audley-front.story: Film the front of the house first. It looks enormous. But most of it was knocked down long ago.
facts: In the 1660s, King Charles the Second bought it, because it was only 20 miles from the horse races at Newmarket. The family got it back in 1701. Then in the 1700s, about two thirds of the house was knocked down.

In 1825, Lord Braybrooke of Audley End published Samuel Pepys's famous diary for the first time. Pepys wrote it in secret shorthand. The code was cracked using his story of King Charles the Second's escape. That's the same king who once owned this house.

routeCard.sub: Audley End · 10:00 AM · about 35 minutes from home
routeCard.note: Book online before midnight on Friday to save up to 15%. The grounds open at 10:00. The house opens at 10:30.

planCard.todo: Say the cold open here. Then the outside shots. The house opens at 10:30.

audley-front.onCamera: This is Audley End. It's enormous. But what you see is only about one third of the original house.
audley-front.closeOnCamera: The man who built this house was in charge of the king's money. And it ended with him in prison. Let's go inside.

audley-house.name: Audley End — the house
audley-house.story: This is the main story of the day: the man in charge of the king's money built a palace to impress the king. Then the money went missing.
facts: There was a monastery here first. In 1538, King Henry the Eighth closed it and gave the land to Thomas Audley. That's why it's called Audley End. Thomas Howard was his grandson.
Howard built this palace to impress the new king, James the First. King James came to see it. He reportedly said that it was too large for a king, but it might do for a Lord Treasurer.

routeCard.note: Last entry to the house is 3:30. Ask at the desk about filming inside.

see: The Polish graffiti in the Coal Gallery
planCard.todo: Ask at the entrance if you can film inside. In the Coal Gallery, film the Polish soldiers' graffiti for later. Walk to the Stable Yard at 11:05.

audley-house.onCamera: This house was built in the early 1600s by Thomas Howard, Earl of Suffolk. He was the Lord Treasurer, the man in charge of King James the First's money.
audley-house.closeOnCamera: And here's how it ended. In 1618, money went missing from the Treasury. In 1619, Howard and his wife were put on trial. They were fined thirty thousand pounds and locked in the Tower of London.

audley-horses.name: The horses and the stables
audley-horses.story: Riding display at 11:15 in the Stable Yard, weather permitting. The website only says 'until October', so it may have finished for the year. The horses live in the stables either way.
facts: They were built around 1610, by Thomas Howard, the same man who built the house. Experts think it was first built as rooms for the servants who travelled with the king. A few years later, it was turned into a stable.
When it became a stable, the big bay windows were added. Experts think they were for the owner and his guests. From there, they could look at the horses and talk about them.

routeCard.sub: The Stable Yard · riding display 11:15 AM
routeCard.note: Free with your ticket. No booking. Weekends at 11:15 and 2:30, weather permitting.

planCard.todo: Be there by 11:10. If there's no display, film the horses in the stables.

audley-horses.onCamera: These stables are more than 400 years old. And horses still live here.
audley-horses.closeOnCamera: Earlier, I told you why King Charles the Second bought this house. It was close to the horse races at Newmarket. So horses are a big part of this house's story.

audley-kitchen.name: The Victorian kitchen
audley-kitchen.angle: A Victorian cook who became a YouTube star
audley-kitchen.story: The service wing shows how the servants lived and worked in the 1880s. The kitchen belonged to a real cook, Avis Crocombe. Today people all over the world know her from YouTube. The costumed cooks stopped in December 2024, so you'll see the kitchen, not her.
facts: Her name was Avis Crocombe. She was the head cook here in the 1880s. Historians found her name in the 1881 census, the official list of everyone living in each house that year.
Her handwritten recipe book survived. A relative found it at the back of a drawer, and gave it to the house.

routeCard.note: The costumed cooks stopped in December 2024. You'll see the kitchen, not a live cook.

planCard.todo: Film the kitchen and tell Mrs Crocombe's story. Then walk out to the park.

audley-kitchen.onCamera: This kitchen belonged to a real Victorian cook. And today, she's a YouTube star.
audley-kitchen.closeOnCamera: English Heritage made a YouTube series about her, called The Victorian Way. An actress plays her, cooking her real recipes. That's why people all over the world know her name.

audley-ww2.name: The secret commando school
audley-ww2.story: In the park, find the memorial urn for the Polish soldiers. Say your open and close there. Use the graffiti you filmed in the Coal Gallery for the voiceover.
facts: The British called it Station 43. From 1942, Polish soldiers learned sabotage, spying and secret radio work here. Their nickname was the Cichociemni. It means 'the Silent Unseen'.
Germany had occupied Poland. 316 of these soldiers parachuted back into Poland, and most of them trained here. More than 100 of them were killed, by the Germans, or later by the communists.

routeCard.sub: The Polish memorial, West Park · 12:30 PM
routeCard.note: In the park, a short walk from the house.

planCard.todo: Open and close at the urn. Then lunch.

audley-ww2.onCamera: In the Second World War, this house was a secret training school for Polish paratroopers.
audley-ww2.closeOnCamera: This urn was put here in 1983, to remember them. And inside the house, a few lines of their graffiti are still on the wall in the Coal Gallery. It's almost all they left behind.

lunch.name: Lunch
lunch.story: Have lunch, then drive 6 minutes to Saffron Walden.

routeCard.note: Saffron Walden is 6 minutes by car.

see: The café at Audley End, or cafés in town
planCard.todo: Lunch, then drive to Saffron Walden. Park in the town centre.

sw-market.name: Market Place and the Saturday market
sw-market.angle: A town named after a spice
sw-market.story: Park in the town centre and walk to the Market Place. On Saturdays there's a market here. Start the story here: the town got rich from saffron, and even changed its name because of it.
facts: Hundreds of years ago, farmers around here grew fields of saffron crocuses. People used saffron to dye cloth yellow. The saffron trade made the town rich.
The town used to be called Chipping Walden. 'Chipping' is an old English word for market. By the 1540s, people were calling it Saffron Walden instead.

routeCard.sub: Saffron Walden · 2:00 PM · 6 minutes from Audley End
routeCard.note: Park in the town centre. The Market Place is a short walk.

see: Old timber houses around the square
planCard.todo: Film the market first. The stalls may start packing up in the afternoon.

sw-market.onCamera: This town is named after a spice: saffron. Saffron comes from a purple crocus flower.
sw-market.closeOnCamera: The town even made a joke about it. Its seal from 1549 shows three crocuses inside castle walls. Saffron, walled in. Saffron Walden.

old-sun.name: The Old Sun Inn
old-sun.story: On Church Street, on your way from the market to the church. It's a shop now, so film the outside. Look at the plaster on the front.
facts: Cromwell was one of the leaders of Parliament's army in the English Civil War. That was a war between King Charles the First and Parliament. In 1647 the army came to Saffron Walden, and Cromwell stayed here.
The building is from the 1300s. Samuel Pepys, the famous diary writer, visited it too.

routeCard.note: It's a shop now. Film the outside and the plaster.

see: The decorated plaster on the front
planCard.todo: Film the front from across the street. Then walk 2 minutes to the church.

old-sun.onCamera: This old building was Oliver Cromwell's headquarters, in May 1647.
old-sun.closeOnCamera: Now look at the plaster on the front. It shows two giants fighting. People think it's the local legend of Tom Hickathrift, a very strong man who killed a giant with a cart axle. But nobody is completely sure.

st-marys.name: St Mary's Church
st-marys.story: Two minutes' walk from the Market Place. This church is huge for a small town. Its size shows how rich saffron made Saffron Walden. It's usually open every day.
facts: It's 56 metres long. Its spire is 59 metres tall, the tallest in Essex. The spire is the newest part. It was added in 1832.
Money from the saffron trade helped pay for it. The church was rebuilt from about 1450, when the town was at its richest.

routeCard.note: Usually open every day. If it's locked, film the outside and the spire.

planCard.todo: Inside first, then the spire from the churchyard. If it's locked, film from outside.

st-marys.onCamera: This is the biggest church in Essex that isn't a cathedral. And it's in a small market town.
st-marys.closeOnCamera: And here's a link to my Cambridge video. One of the master builders here was John Wastell. He also built King's College Chapel in Cambridge. That's why this church might look familiar.

turf-maze.name: The Turf Maze
turf-maze.angle: A maze cut into the grass
turf-maze.story: About 8 minutes' walk east, on the Common. It's not a hedge maze. It's a pattern cut into the grass, and it's very old. It's free and always open.
facts: It has 17 rings. It's one of the largest old turf mazes in Europe.
Nobody knows exactly how old it is. Historians think it probably comes from the Middle Ages.

routeCard.sub: The Common · 3:30 PM · about 8 minutes' walk
routeCard.note: Free. At the east end of the Common.

planCard.todo: Walk the maze while you talk. Say the sign-off here. Then back to the car and drive home.

turf-maze.onCamera: This maze isn't made of hedges. It's cut into the grass.
turf-maze.closeOnCamera: The first time it appears in writing is 1699. That year, the town paid 15 shillings to have it cut again. So people have looked after this maze for more than 300 years.

coldOpen.title: Cold open
facts: The hook: 'Today: a house so big that its builder ended up in prison, and a town named after a spice.'
What this is: Audley End in the morning, and Saffron Walden in the afternoon.
The promise: 'That house has more secrets. Horses in 400-year-old stables. A Victorian cook who is now a YouTube star. And a secret school for Polish soldiers in the Second World War.'

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
facts: Where you are: at the Turf Maze in Saffron Walden.
The recap: the king's money built that house, Polish soldiers trained there in secret, and saffron made this town rich.
The ask: like and subscribe, and tell me where I should go next.
